messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
M is complete and (F_n) is a sequence of nonempty closed subsets with F_{n+1}\subset F_n and diam F_n\to0.
For each n there is x_n\in F_n, and d(x_m,x_n)\le diam F_n for m>n, so (x_n) is Cauchy.
Completeness yields x_n\to x, and closedness with F_{n+1}\subset F_n gives x\in F_n for all n, hence \bigcap_n F_n\neq\varnothing.
Conversely, if every such nested family has nonempty intersection, then for a Cauchy sequence (y_n) the closed tails F_n=\overline{\{y_k:k\ge n\}} are nested, nonempty, closed, have diameters tending to 0, and any x in \bigcap F_n satisfies d(x,y_n)\le diam F_n.
Does the assumed property then force some x to lie in all F_n?
Does that x serve as the limit of the Cauchy sequence?
